Prudent

PROO-dent -- shares a root with 'provident,' meaning to plan ahead wisely. · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Prudent is showing care and good judgment, especially about practical matters; sensible.

Waiting until the storm passed before driving home was the prudent decision.

Worked Example

Before signing the lease, a young renter carefully reads every clause, asks the landlord several questions, and calculates whether the rent truly fits her monthly budget.

That careful, sensible weighing of a decision before acting is exactly what prudent means. Unlike 'lucky,' which is about chance, prudent describes deliberate good judgment.

How Prudent Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

judicious

judicious: having or showing good judgment

sensible

sensible: having practical good sense

cautious

cautious: careful to avoid danger or mistakes

Antonyms

reckless

reckless: without thought for the consequences of an action

rash

rash: acting without careful thought

How Strong Is It? — sensible → prudent → judicious

sensible vs. prudent

sensible vs. prudent: Sensible is a more everyday word than prudent -- sensible just means showing good sense in daily choices, while prudent carries a more formal, deliberate weighing of risk.

judicious vs. prudent

judicious vs. prudent: Judicious can feel even more careful than prudent: prudent suggests general good sense, while judicious specifically implies a careful, almost judge-like weighing of a decision.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — prud-

root — prud-: foresight, practical wisdom (Latin (prudentia, from providentia))

suffix — -ent

suffix — -ent: doing or being; forms an adjective (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: Latin prudentia meant 'foresight, practical wisdom' -- shortened from providentia, 'seeing ahead' -- and the suffix -ent forms the adjective. A prudent person is one who sees ahead and plans wisely.

Use the root in a new word: provident

Use the root in a new word: provident: Their provident planning meant the family had savings set aside for years of college tuition.
